newsitem.title: EGYPT: World Bank may help Egyptian desert scheme.
newsitem.headline: World Bank may help Egyptian desert scheme.

text.p: The World Bank may help the Egyptian government on an ambitious project to irrigate 500,000 acres (200,000 hectares) in the Western desert with water from the Nile, a World Bank official said on Monday.
Operations officer Badr Kamel said a World Bank mission would visit Egypt within two weeks to look into the scheme.

"They will see how we can help in this project," he added. The head of the mission will be Salah Darghouth, the bank's division chief for natural resources, water and environment in the Middle East and North Africa.

It is too early to say what form cooperation would take, such as finance or technical assistance, Kamel said. But in principle, if Egypt wants to borrow from the World Bank, the bank is ready to lend, he added.
Egypt, after years of fighting to reduce its foreign debt from the crippling levels of the 1980s, has been reluctant to borrow abroad in large amounts, bankers say.
But the desert irrigation project is expected to cost at least $810 million over the next four years and Finance Minister Mohieddin el-Gharib says the money will not come from budget.
Government newspapers on Monday quoted Agriculture Minister Youssef Wali as saying the World Bank was ready to help carry out the desert project.

He contrasted this to the bank's refusal to finance the Aswan High Dam back in the 1950s. The bank's refusal, under U.S. pressure, was an important factor in Egypt nationalising the Suez Canal and turning to the Soviet Union for help.
